---
title: "Mini-Project #01"
---

```{r}
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event) |>
    rename(hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`, 
          release_date  = `Release Date`,
          available_globally = `Available Globally?`) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(year),
           available_globally = available_globally == "Yes")
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```


**Task 4: Initial EDA Pass**
```{r}
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)

summary(NETFLIX_DATA)

library(skimr)
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```



**Task 5: Exploratory Questions - Inline Values**

**1. What date range is covered by this data set?**

The dataset covers Netflix movie data from `r NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(min(period_start,na.rm = TRUE))` to `r NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(max(period_end, na.rm=TRUE))`.


**2. How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set? (Don’t worry about combining seasons for now: you can treat “Stranger Things 2” and “Stranger Things 3” as different shows.)**

There are `r n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$Title)` different shows and movies covered in this dataset.


**3. How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the Bridgerton universe?**

The total hours spent watching shows from the *Bridgerton* universe is `r format(NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(str_detect(Title, "Bridgerton")) |> summarize(total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(total_hours), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` hours.


**4. How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things? For this question, we only want the “real” Stranger Things shows and not the companion behind-the-scenes show (“Beyond Stranger Things”), the animated spin-off (“Tales from ’85”), or the background music (“Stranger Things: Fireplace”).**

The total number of hours spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things is `r format(NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(str_detect(Title, "Stranger Things")) |> filter_out(str_detect(Title, "Beyond Stranger Things")) |> filter_out(str_detect(Title, "Tales from '85")) |> filter_out(str_detect(Title, "Fireplace")) |> summarize(total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(total_hours), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` hours.

**5. What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?**

The total time spent on the Top 10 Titles of 2026H1 is `r NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> arrange(desc(hours_viewed)) |> summarize(percentage = scales::percent(sum(head(hours_viewed, 10), na.rm = TRUE) / sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.01)) |>pull(percentage)`.
                                            
**6. What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)**

Netflix’s catalog is globally available for 
`r NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(by_title = scales::percent(mean(available_globally, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.01), weighted_by_hours = scales::percent(sum(hours_viewed[available_globally], na.rm = TRUE) / sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.01))`, repectively, by title and weighted by hours viewed.


**Task 6: Exploratory Questions - Table Answers**

**1. What was the top title (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?**

``` {r}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

top_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    viewership_fraction = hours_viewed / total_hours
  ) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    Period = period,
    `Top Title` = Title,
    `Hours Viewed` = hours_viewed,
    `Fraction of Viewership` = viewership_fraction
  )

top_titles |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = `Hours Viewed`,
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = `Fraction of Viewership`,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Period = "Reporting Period",
    `Top Title` = "Top Title",
    `Hours Viewed` = "Total Hours Viewed",
    `Fraction of Viewership` = "Share of Viewership"
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Most-Watched Netflix Title by Period",
    subtitle = "Top title and share of total hours viewed"
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

**2. How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.**
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

catalog_size <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_titles = n_distinct(Title),
    total_runtime_hours = sum(Runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(period)

catalog_size |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    number_of_titles = "Number of Titles",
    total_runtime_hours = "Total Runtime (Hours)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = number_of_titles,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = total_runtime_hours,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Catalog Size Over Time",
    subtitle = "Number of titles and total runtime by reporting period"
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

**3. Which titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back on as ‘comfort food’, e.g., re-runs of Friends.**
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

staple_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    rank = min_rank(desc(hours_viewed))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(Title) |>
  summarise(
    periods_present = n_distinct(period),
    top_10_periods = sum(rank <= 10),
    average_rank = mean(rank, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_hours_viewed = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    desc(periods_present),
    desc(top_10_periods),
    average_rank
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 15)

staple_titles |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Title = "Title",
    periods_present = "Periods Present",
    top_10_periods = "Top 10 Appearances",
    average_rank = "Average Rank",
    average_hours_viewed = "Average Hours Viewed"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = average_rank,
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = average_hours_viewed,
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix's Most Consistent Titles",
    subtitle = "Identifying potential viewer comfort-food favorites"
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

**4. Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?**

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

show_movie_share <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(Title, regex("\\bseason\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)) |
        Runtime > 240,
      "Shows",
      "Movies"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarise(
    hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    fraction = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, content_type, fraction) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = content_type,
    values_from = fraction
  ) |>
  arrange(period)

show_movie_share |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Reporting Period",
    Shows = "TV Shows",
    Movies = "Movies"
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(Shows, Movies),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Viewing by Content Type",
    subtitle = "Share of total hours viewed in each reporting period"
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

**5. How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?**
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

# Compare average viewership across content types
live_comparison <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Events", "Pre-taped")
  ) |>
  group_by(content_type) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_titles = n(),
    average_hours_viewed = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours_viewed = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

live_comparison |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    content_type = "Content Type",
    number_of_titles = "Number of Entries",
    average_hours_viewed = "Average Hours Viewed",
    median_hours_viewed = "Median Hours Viewed"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(average_hours_viewed, median_hours_viewed),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Live Events vs. Pre-taped Content",
    subtitle = "Viewership across all reporting periods"
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

**Task 7: Corporate Strategy Memo**

To: Netflix Leadership Team

**Corporate strategy memo addressed to Netflix leadership**

With the analysis done above, it should be noted that Netflix should prioritize globally available contents while maintaining a strong focus on successful TV shows. Total viewerships suggest that globally available titles accounts for a significant amount of total viewing hours from the entire Netflix catalog. TV shows account for substantially more viewings tan movies. These findings support a strategy on Netflix’s future focus on international audience engagement.

Our analysis indicates that 35.09% of the Netflix's catalog is globally available, which accounted for 51.92% of the total hours viewed. As the globally available titles are capturing more than a half of the total viewership, it gives a signal that Netflix’s globally available titles are significantly more popular than regional-licensed contents.

This indicates that large share of Netflix’s audience engages more in globally available titles in their catalog. For 2027 and beyond, Netlix should prioritize productions with international contents and invest more in global marketing and subtitling to meet the needs of global audience. By expanding the market globally, Netflix should be able to attract more audience across multiple markets and capture more viewerships. While global recognition is important, regionally licensed contents are as important. Global reach should not come at the expense of regional content. Regionally licensed distributions are important for reflecting local cultures, meets the preference of a specific group of audience. This could strengthen Netflix’s presence in the specific markets. Therefore, Netflix should pursue a balanced content strategy that combines globally recognizable titles within regionally licensed content. By leveraging the strengths of both categories, Netflix can expand its international audience while maintaining strong engagement across local markets.

During reporting period 2023H1 to the most recent period 2026H1, our analysis suggests that TV shows account for approximately 69.17% to 96.46%% of total viewing hours, compared to only 2.88% to 4.17% on movies. Other classified content types only account for approximately 0.116% to 0.279%, which is considered relatively minimal. These findings suggest that TV shows are the primary drivers of viewing activity on Netflix, and Netflix should continue to invest in these outstanding series to sustain audience engagement across different seasons.

From the ‘Netflix’s Most Consistent Titles’ table, the viewer’s comfort-food favorites is Stranger Things 4, which has averaged 207,385,714 hours viewed. This is an example where the high performing series are attracting substantial viewership, as evidenced by the top show being a 4th season of a TV show series. In 2027, Netflix should continue investing in these successful TV shows, develop compelling and interesting storylines across seasons and identify potential opportunities. While continuing to invest in new seasons of the successful TV shows, Netflix should also explore opportunities to strengthen its movies content. Although movies only account for a small share of the total viewing house, they also attract difference audience segments. By balancing investment in successful TV shows and movie acquisition, Netflix could expand to a larger range of viewer preference and maximize the reach of overall audience in different segments.
